relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: A prophet crosses the divided border to confront the altar where royal religion is being consolidated.
His oracle imagines future reform through slain priests and burned bones, a vision carrying its own violence.
The altar's fracture is offered as confirmation.
Jeroboam reaches to seize the speaker, and his hand becomes unable to return.
The altar splits while its ashes spill.
The threatened prophet prays for the king who tried to arrest him, and the hand is restored.
The king responds with hospitality and reward.
The prophet refuses even half the royal house.
His boundary is specific: no food, no water, no return by the same road.
He leaves by another path.
An older prophet hears the entire public story through his sons.
He asks not whether to intervene but which road the traveler took.
His sons prepare the donkey that will carry him into the stranger's path.
He finds the man resting beneath a tree and confirms his identity.
The invitation appears simple: come home and eat.
The traveler repeats his refusal.
He explains the boundary through the word he received.
The elder claims prophetic equality and angelic authorization, but the narrator names the claim a lie.
Trust in spiritual authority leads the traveler back across his own boundary.
At the table, a genuine word now comes through the person who deceived him.
The oracle places responsibility upon the manipulated guest rather than the lying host.
His burial among ancestors is denied because he ate and drank after being deceived.
The deceiver prepares the animal that carries the traveler toward death.
A lion kills him, while lion and donkey remain beside the body in an eerie stillness.
Passersby witness the impossible scene and carry news into town.
The old prophet interprets the death as fulfilled punishment without first confessing his own lie.
He returns to the road.
The untouched corpse and living donkey make the event read as sign rather than ordinary predation.
The old prophet retrieves the person his deception helped endanger.
He mourns him as brother and provides his own tomb.
He asks that their bones eventually rest together.
He still trusts the first prophet's public word against Bethel.
Jeroboam continues building a priesthood open to anyone he appoints.
The royal religious system moves toward its narrated destruction.

contemplative_note: The chapter's clearest discernment lesson is not terror of making one wrong move. It is that spiritual authority can lie, invoke angels, override boundaries, and then interpret the resulting harm as the victim's fault. A trustworthy path makes room for verification, consent, accountability, and mercy.
